blocks.text: Latin verbs are divided into five conjugations; in addition to the three that you have already learned there is a fourth conjugation and a ‘mixed’ conjugation with characteristics of both third and fourth conjugations. The mixed conjugation is also called ‘third conjugation in -iō’ or ‘third conjugation i-stems’. These verbs are conjugated as follows:
The imperative of faciō is irregular: fac, facite.

header: Fourth conjugation audiō, audīre, audīvī, audītum ‘hear’
Mixed conjugation capiō, capere, cēpī, captum ‘take’, ‘capture’
rows: regite Third conjugation regō, regere, rēxī, rēctum ‘rule’ (for comparison)
audīte Fourth conjugation audiō, audīre, audīvī, audītum ‘hear’
capite Mixed conjugation capiō, capere, cēpī, captum ‘take’, ‘capture’

blocks.text: As with the first and second conjugations, in the perfect indicative and imperfect subjunctive these verbs take exactly the same endings as the third-conjugation verbs.
In the present and future indicative and in the present subjunctive they also take the same endings, with the addition of an -iwherever there is not already an -i-.

Like verbs of the first three conjugations, fourth-conjugation verbs can be identified by their second principal parts: their infinitives end in -īre. Mixed-conjugation verbs are trickier to spot, since their second principal parts end in -ere like those of thirdconjugation verbs: one has to use the combination of a first principal part in -iō (which third-conjugation verbs never have, though fourth-conjugation ones do) and a second principal part in -ere (which fourth-conjugation verbs never have, though thirdconjugation ones do) to identify verbs of the mixed conjugation.
Identify the conjugations to which each of these verbs belongs:
moenia reficiamus ne hostes urbem capiant.
moenia refecimus ne hostes urbem caperent.
moenia reficiemus ne hostes urbem capiant.
frater meus multas oves vendidit ut pecuniam haberet.
frater meus multas oves vendet ut pecunicam habeat.
frater, oves vende ut pecuniam habeas!
ille ad urbem venit ut sororem inveniat.
ille ad urbem venit ut sororem inveniret.
hic ad urbem veniet ut sororem inveniat.
hic ad urbem veniat ut sororem inveniat.
veniamus ad urbem ut sororem inveniamus.
veni ad urbem ut sororem invenias!
hi ad oppidum veniunt ut patrem sepeliant.
hi ad oppidum venerunt ut patrem sepelirent.
The citizens came to the city to hear the king’s words.
The citizens will come to the city in order to hear the king’s words.
The citizens are coming to the city to hear the king’s words.
Let the citizens come to the city to hear the king’s words.
Citizens, come to the city to hear the king’s words!
Who has repaired the walls? Let’s praise that man!
To whom should I give those animals?
The soldiers repaired our walls to hinder the enemy.
Let the soldiers repair our walls in order to hinder the enemy.
The soldiers will repair our walls so that they will hinder the enemy.
Whose mother heard you? yours? mine?
The enemy came across the river to conquer our men.
The enemy is coming across the river to conquer our men.
The enemy will come across the river in order to conquer our men.
To which brother did you give my book? You have five brothers!
What have you buried in my field?
Colloquium Harleianum 6d–f (adapted): continuation of the school scene in the preceding chapter.
